extracted.intended_audience: writers, translators, dramatists, and literary critics (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating satirical pieces, dramatic writing, and translations—focusing on targets of satire, decency of allusion, audience effects, and fidelity in translation. Emphasizes moral/ethical tone and methods for moving readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: expose only what is corrigible and discriminate targets
rubrics_metrics.description: A Satyr should expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not level an entire species or class with universal censure ("Such levelling Satyrs are of no Use to the World"). Effective satire should single out faults that can be corrected and distinguish rightful objects of satire from those undeserving of it (context: contrast with Juvenal and Boileau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity: preserve sentiments over literalness
rubrics_metrics.description: I have translated the Author very faithfully, and if not Word for Word (which our Language would not bear) at least so as to comprehend every one of his Sentiments, without adding any thing of my own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating, aim to convey the original author's meanings and sentiments even if a word-for-word rendering is impossible or would be awkward in the target language; avoid inserting your own ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe bienséance (decency) in allusions and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: the Rule of observing what the French call the _bienséance_, in an Allusion... the Ancients, provided there was a Likeness in their Similitudes, did not much trouble themselves about the Decency of the Comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern taste (per the essay) expects decency and propriety in comparisons/allusions; adapt allusions to contemporary standards of decorum even if ancient models were less scrupulous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to move proper passions rather than appetites or cheap mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Appetites are sooner moved than the Passions: A sly Expression which alludes to Bawdry, puts a whole Row into a pleasing Smirk; when a good Sentence that describes an inward Sentiment of the Soul, is received with the greatest Coldness and Indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writing that evokes deep emotions (pity, generosity, moral concern) over devices that elicit shallow titillation or laughter rooted in bawdry. Be mindful that audiences often respond more readily to coarse stimuli than to genuine passion; craft incidents and phrasing to overcome that tendency (stage examples: tragic moments met with laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of audience dispositions and how they read theatrical moments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a melancholy Prospect when we see a numerous Assembly lost to all serious Entertainments... the whole Audience is afraid of letting fall a Tear, and shun as a Weakness the best and worthiest Part of our Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and dramatists should be aware of the audience's prevailing tastes, social performance, and pressures (e.g., fear of appearing weak). Structure scenes and signals to guide the audience towards intended emotional responses, recognizing that social dynamics in the house can suppress sincere reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: avoid ostentation; modesty preserves esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Call upon Mankind to value and esteem those who set a moderate Price upon their own Merit... It were therefore a just Rule, to keep your Desires, your Words and Actions, within the Regard you observe your Friends have for you; and never, if it were in a Man's Power, to take as much as he possibly might either in Preferment or Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portraying characters or adopting a narrative voice, restraint and modesty produce sympathy and moral authority. Overstated pretension or habitual arrogance in speech/behavior risks alienating readers and undermining character credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative depiction of ages and manners to enlighten readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reader cannot be more rationally entertained, than by comparing the Virtues and Vices of his own Times with those which prevailed in the Times of his Forefathers; and drawing a Parallel in his Mind between his own private Character, and that of other Persons...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ contrasts across periods, cultures, or character types to illuminate moral lessons, shock complacency, and encourage self-reflection; variety in depiction of manners enhances reader engagement and critical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad, indiscriminate satire of whole groups (no 'levelling' satires)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such levelling Satyrs are of no Use to the World... what Vice or Frailty can a Discourse correct, which censures the whole Species alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective moral or satirical critique must be targeted and constructive; wholesale denunciation of entire groups is unhelpful and corrosive. Distinguish between individuals and systemic/correctable faults.
